tier_reason: The Cloudflare blog post (2016-04-04) gives first-party cycles/byte graphs against OpenSSL 1.1.0-pre on an unnamed Haswell CPU. It states 'the average performance advantage is 7%' and 'below 2 cycles/byte', but it names no compiler or flags, no exact CPU model, and no benchmark code, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page: 'significantly outperforms OpenSSL [1.1.0-pre] for short records, and is slightly faster for longer records. The average performance advantage is 7%' (average across the 64 B to 16 KB record sizes graphed; cycles/byte for 'seal' with 13 bytes AAD on Haswell; graphs only, not tabulated). The page also says it gets 'below 2 cycles/byte' for large records. AES-128-GCM and AES-256-GCM still beat ChaCha20-Poly1305 for records larger than 320 bytes.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are read off graphs in a 2016-04-04 blog post, not tabulated. Compiler, flags and exact CPU model ('a Haswell CPU') are not stated, so tier is capped at C. The baseline was pre-release OpenSSL 1.1.0, and the page does not say whether that baseline was generic C or assembly. The repository is mainly Cloudflare's nginx cipher configuration. The speed code is patches/openssl__chacha20_poly1305_draft_and_rfc_ossl102{f,g,j}.patch (Vlad Krasnov; adds an AVX2 chacha20_poly1305_x86_64.pl) against OpenSSL 1.0.2. The openssl__1.1.0_chacha20_poly1305.patch only changes cipher-preference logic in ssl/s3_lib.c. The same stitched assembly (Copyright 2015 CloudFlare, author Vlad Krasnov) is in BoringSSL crypto/cipher_extra/asm/chacha20_poly1305_x86_64.pl. Inclusion in upstream OpenSSL was not verified. The patches modify OpenSSL-licensed files, so the repository's BSD-3-Clause license does not cover the whole patched tree. This is mainly a historical result, not a current 'faster than OpenSSL' claim.

notes: The record's '7% for short TLS records' misattributes the figure. The page gives 7% as the average over all sizes and calls the short-record gain 'significant'. The caveat's '2015' date is wrong: the post is dated 2016-04-04. Last commit is 2024-09-16, so status is stale, not finished. gh api was rate-limited, so metadata comes from the github.com pages (BSD-3-Clause, 1313 stars, not archived).

tier_reason: The EuroBSDCon 2019 slides only compare software kTLS (68% CPU) with T6 NIC kTLS (35% CPU) at 90 Gb/s. The Netflix AsiaBSDCon 2015 paper does compare against userspace nginx+OpenSSL on the same appliance with live traffic: about 8.5 Gbps versus about 9 Gbps with in-kernel TLS sendfile. These are first-party production numbers with no benchmark code or compiler details, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Netflix AsiaBSDCon 2015 paper (early in-kernel TLS prototype, 'SSLsendfile'): the same OCA Rev D serving real Netflix traffic with AES-GCM did 'about 9Gps' with in-kernel bulk encryption versus 'about 8.5GPS' with userspace nginx+OpenSSL (~1.06x, derived from page data). The authors call this 'a slight performance improvement'. The later EuroBSDCon 2019 FreeBSD 13 kTLS slides give only 90 Gb/s at 68% CPU (software kTLS) versus 35% CPU (Chelsio T6 NIC kTLS offload), with no userspace-OpenSSL number.
corrections.workload: 2015 paper: Netflix OpenConnect Appliance serving real Netflix video traffic over TLS, nginx preferring AES-NI AES-GCM, with a sysctl toggling in-kernel TLS sendfile against plain userspace OpenSSL on the same firmware image, measured over a night of production traffic. 2019 slides: Netflix nginx video serving at 90 Gb/s, comparing CPU use of software kTLS against Chelsio T6 NIC kTLS offload.
corrections.hardware: 2015 comparison: Netflix OCA 'Rev D', Intel Xeon E5-2650L (exact version not stated), 64 GB RAM, FreeBSD 10.1, nginx 1.5. 2019 slides: Intel Xeon E5-2697A v4 @ 2.60GHz (16 core/32 HTT), 128GB DDR4-2400, 1x100GbE (T6 NIC), 4x NVMe.
corrections.stars_or_usage: GitHub mirror freebsd/freebsd-src has 9,335 stars; kernel kTLS support added in r351522 (FreeBSD 13); used in production at Netflix
corrections.caveats: The only measured head-to-head against userspace OpenSSL (about 8.5 to about 9 Gbps, ~6%, read from the 2015 paper text) is for Netflix's early FreeBSD 10 prototype. That prototype still made an extra copy through the Open Crypto Framework, so it is not the FreeBSD 13 kTLS code now in freebsd-src (uipc_ktls.c, Copyright 2014-2019 Netflix). The 2019 slides compare software kTLS with NIC-offload kTLS only and argue the OpenSSL advantage qualitatively. The numbers are from live production traffic with no public benchmark harness or compiler details, so tier is capped at C. The kTLS files carry an SPDX BSD-2-Clause header. The repository-level license is NOASSERTION because FreeBSD mixes licenses.

notes: The given benchmark_url has no numbers against the named OpenSSL baseline. I repointed benchmark_url to the Netflix AsiaBSDCon 2015 paper, which does measure against userspace nginx+OpenSSL, though only for a precursor prototype. The Netflix tech blog post on kTLS (Medium) returned 403 and was not read. gh api was rate-limited, so metadata comes from github.com pages (9335 stars, not archived, last commit on main 2026-09-26; uipc_ktls.c last changed 2026-09-23).

tier_reason: The paper appeared at USENIX Security '22 (peer-reviewed; artifact badges Available, Functional and Reproduced). Its Section 4.4 and Figure 5 show sntrup761 and sntrup857 completing more TLS 1.3 connections/sec than OpenSSL 1.1.1k's ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256, with tls_timer code public and CPUs named. Compiler and flags are not stated, so not A. This upgrades the record from C to B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: USENIX Security '22 paper, Section 4.4 and Figure 5: over 100 samples of 8192 sequential TLS 1.3 handshakes each, sntrup761 and sntrup857 'consistently achieve more connections per second' than OpenSSL 1.1.1k's ASM-optimized X25519 and P-256. The results are shown only as CDF curves on a 440-620 connections/sec axis, with no tabulated numbers. Key generation: sntrup761 batch keygen (batch size 32) costs 156317 amortized Haswell cycles per key, versus 814608 for the previous best sntrup761 software and 269191 for CECPQ2's ntruhrss701 (~1.72x versus ntruhrss701, derived from page data). The ntruhrss701 comparison is against the CECPQ2 KEM, not against OpenSSL.
corrections.caveats: The paper was published at USENIX Security 2022 (confirmed on the usenix.org presentation page, with Available, Functional and Reproduced artifact badges). The headline 'more handshakes/sec' result is shown only as a CDF plot, not a tabulated number. The authors warn that 'one should not conclude that sntrup761 and sntrup857 cost less than ECC overall', because the unloaded Gigabit LAN hides the larger lattice communication costs. The 156317-cycle figure is the amortized cost of batch key generation (batch of 32); unbatched sntrup761 keygen is 819332 cycles (Table 3). Licensing is mixed: engntru is LGPL-3.0-or-later (COPYING and COPYING.LESSER), tls_timer is Apache-2.0 (LICENSE), and the speed-critical libsntrup761 tarball has no license file or statement (only build and test harness files say 'Public domain'). The OpenSSL patches modify OpenSSL 1.1.1 code. The demo page was last updated 2021.12.14 (OpenSSL 1.1.1m patch); the library tarballs are dated 2021-06-08.

notes: The given demo.html only carries the 156317-cycle keygen figure. The X25519/P-256 handshake comparison is in the paper, and the 269191 ntruhrss701 figure is on the intro page and in paper Table 1, so I repointed benchmark_url to the paper PDF. The venue is confirmed as USENIX Security '22, which moves the tier from C to B. The record's claim that no license exists in the tarballs is wrong for engntru (LGPL-3.0+) and tls_timer (Apache-2.0). I kept usability 'reference' because the core libsntrup761 is unlicensed, and set status to abandoned because the last update was more than 3 years ago and the authors do not say the work is complete.
